KUBERNETES RESOURCE LIMITS CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Will this container take down its whole node?

Paste or load Kubernetes manifest YAML and get a deterministic report of every container missing a memory limit, memory request, CPU request, or ephemeral-storage limit -- the specific gaps that let one container starve or crowd out everything else sharing its node.

Nothing is uploaded. The file you load is read in this browser and never leaves your device. No kubeconfig, no API server call.

1. Load your manifests

2. What this manifest could do to its node

WorkloadContainerSeverityFindingFix

Prefer a CLI, or want this as a CI gate before you deploy?

Same checks, zero dependencies, one file — run it against your manifest repo or your Helm/Kustomize render output:

node cli.mjs check manifests.yaml                    # list every finding, exit 0 (informational)
node cli.mjs check manifests.yaml --fail-on-risk     # exit 1 if any container is left unbounded or invalid
node cli.mjs check manifests.yaml --fail-on-risk --json

Get cli.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install. It reads only the local file you name: no network call, ever.

What this checks — and what it cannot

Six checks, run against every container and init container in every Pod, Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, ReplicaSet, Job, and CronJob it finds: a missing memory limit or request, a missing CPU request, a missing ephemeral-storage limit, a CPU limit (reported informational, not a problem — see below), and a request set above its own limit for CPU or memory. See why each one matters for the exact Kubernetes mechanism behind it, sourced from Kubernetes' own documentation rather than assumed.

It cannot see what a container actually uses at runtime — only what the manifest declares — so it cannot tell you whether a number you did set is the right number, only whether one is present and internally consistent. Pair it with kubectl top or your metrics stack for that. Already using Polaris from Fairwinds? See how this checker differs. Wondering whether a visual review of the YAML already covers this? See this checker vs. reading the manifest by eye. Checking a chart rendered by Helm specifically? See Helm Values Schema Check. A manifest passing this check can still drop live traffic during a rollout for reasons that have nothing to do with resource limits — see Kubernetes Rollout Safety Check for readiness probes, PodDisruptionBudgets, and termination grace periods, and Kubernetes Deprecated API Check for whether the manifest survives your next cluster upgrade at all.

Common questions

Why does a missing resource limit matter if my container has never had a problem?

Because the failure a missing limit invites is not gradual, it is a threshold: nothing looks wrong until the node runs low on memory or disk, and then the kubelet's eviction or the kernel's OOM killer acts -- and neither of those is scoped to only the container that grew. A container running fine today with no memory limit is one noisy neighbour away from taking others down with it.

Is my manifest uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser page parses a pasted or locally loaded file entirely in your own browser and never sends it anywhere. The CLI reads only a local file -- no network call, ever.

Does this need a kubeconfig or talk to my cluster?

No. It reads only the YAML text you give it. It has no kubeconfig, makes no API server call, and needs no cluster access at all -- that is what makes it safe to run against production manifests in CI.

Why is a CPU limit reported as informational instead of a problem to fix?

Because, unlike the other findings here, a CPU limit is not simply missing something safer -- once set, it is enforced by the kernel's CFS bandwidth controller, which can throttle a container that bursts within one scheduling period even while the node overall has spare CPU. That is a real, well-documented trade-off (tracked upstream as kubernetes/kubernetes#67577), not a bug, so this tool surfaces it rather than telling you to remove it.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not infrastructure, security, or capacity-planning advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional or Kubernetes' own documentation. It reports what the manifest declares against a fixed set of documented mechanisms -- it cannot know what your workload actually needs at runtime. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for load-testing any limit you set. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get cli.mjs and run it yourself.

Everything runs in your browser. The manifest you load is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded, file_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Limits are one part of a pod spec: Kubernetes Pod Security Check reads the same manifests for privileged containers, hostPath mounts, root users and a missing securityContext.

Free and open source. If this saved you some digging, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-polaris.html.text:
← Back to Kubernetes Resource Limits Check

This checker vs. Polaris

Polaris, maintained by Fairwinds, is an open-source policy engine for Kubernetes covering 30+ built-in best-practice checks -- resource requests and limits among them, alongside security context, health checks, image tag pinning, networking, and more -- with the option to add custom checks defined in JSON Schema. It is deployed: as a dashboard that scores a cluster against its policies, as an admission controller that can reject or modify a non-conforming workload before it is ever created, or as a CLI wired into a CI/CD pipeline to check local YAML files.

This checker answers one narrower question with no deployment step at all. It is a zero-dependency, zero-install browser page and a single Node file: paste or load workload YAML and get a report of which containers are missing a memory limit, memory request, CPU request, or ephemeral-storage limit, which have a request set above their own limit, and which set a CPU limit worth being aware of. It has no admission-controller mode, no cluster dashboard, and nothing to deploy: node cli.mjs check manifests.yaml.

Which one answers your question

What you are trying to doWhere to do it
Enforce resource-limit policy (and 30+ other best practices) continuously across a live cluster, rejecting non-conforming workloads at admission. Polaris -- that is its built-in admission-controller mode.
Score an entire cluster's existing workloads against a broad policy set and track the score over time. Polaris -- that is its dashboard mode.
Check security context, image tags, health checks, or networking config alongside resource limits. Polaris -- this checker covers resource limits only, deliberately.
Check one manifest file with nothing to deploy or install, and nothing uploaded anywhere. This checker -- open the page, paste or load the file, done.
Add a CI gate that is a single committed file with no external binary or cluster connection to set up. This checker -- cli.mjs is the whole dependency.
Understand why a CPU limit specifically can throttle a container even on an idle node, before deciding whether to set one. This checker's own explanation page -- Polaris flags the field but does not walk through the CFS mechanism.

These compose rather than compete. A team already running Polaris as an admission controller loses nothing by also keeping this narrower, install-free checker around for a contributor to run against a manifest before it is even proposed -- catching the same class of gap earlier and for free. And a team that does not want to deploy a dashboard or an admission controller just to check resource requests and limits on a handful of manifests can reach for this instead, with nothing to set up at all. Neither replaces the other; they trade breadth and continuous enforcement for zero deployment cost in opposite directions.

Common questions

Should I use this checker or Polaris?

They sit at different scopes. Polaris is a policy engine covering 30+ Kubernetes best-practice checks -- resource requests/limits among them, alongside security context, image tags, health checks, and more -- deployed as a dashboard, an admission controller, or a CLI wired into CI/CD. This tool checks one narrow thing: whether a workload's memory limit, memory request, CPU request, and ephemeral-storage limit are present, plus whether a request exceeds its own limit. If you want broad, ongoing policy enforcement across a cluster or a whole manifest repository, Polaris is built for that. If you want a single YAML file checked right now with nothing to deploy or install, this is built for that instead.

Does Polaris already cover what this checks?

For the resource-requests/limits question specifically, yes -- both are checking the same underlying Kubernetes fields. Polaris covers that as part of a much broader policy set (30+ built-in checks spanning security, networking, health checks, and image configuration, plus custom checks you can define with JSON Schema), and can enforce it continuously as an admission controller so a non-conforming workload never lands in the cluster at all. This tool covers only the resource-limits question, with no deployment step: paste or load a manifest and get a report immediately.

Why not just deploy Polaris instead of using another tool?

Because they cost different amounts of setup for a narrow, one-off question. Polaris is deployed infrastructure -- a dashboard or admission controller running in or against your cluster, or a CLI you install and wire into a pipeline -- which is exactly the right shape for continuous, cluster-wide policy enforcement. This tool is one dependency-free JavaScript file: node cli.mjs check manifests.yaml, nothing to deploy, nothing to install beyond Node itself. If a team already runs Polaris for its broader policy coverage, this does not replace that -- it is a lighter option for a single manifest someone wants checked before it ever reaches Polaris or a cluster at all.

Is this page affiliated with Polaris or Fairwinds?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Polaris or Fairwinds, named here only to describe what this checker is and is not. What Polaris currently checks and how it is licensed are described on its own documentation and repository -- check there for what it covers today.

Only point either tool at a manifest or cluster you own or are authorised to test. That rule is unchanged by which one you pick.

← Back to the checker

No warranty. This is not infrastructure or capacity-planning advice. It reports what a manifest declares against a fixed set of documented mechanisms -- it cannot know what your workload actually needs at runtime. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. See the disclaimer on the checker itself for the full text.

vs-reading-the-manifest-by-eye.html.text:
← Kubernetes Resource Limits Check

This checker vs. reading the manifest by eye

Skimming a Deployment or StatefulSet's YAML during review is the default first pass, and every team already does it. It reliably misses a container whose resources block has some fields set but not the one that matters, and a request that exceeds its own limit two lines away -- exactly what this free tool checks automatically.

What reading the manifest in review involves

Reviewing a pull request that touches a Deployment or StatefulSet usually means scrolling to the resources block, confirming it exists, and moving on -- especially once a change has already passed a glance at everything else (image tag, replica count, probes). A block with real numbers in it reads as "resourced" at a glance, whether or not every field Kubernetes actually cares about is present.

That works well for a resources block that is missing outright, or an obviously malformed value. It works less well for a block with some fields set -- nothing about a container with a memory request calls attention to the memory limit it is missing -- or for two values that need to be compared against each other rather than read on their own, such as a CPU request under requests and a CPU limit under limits, sitting in different blocks.

The two gaps a visual review is most likely to let through.
What mattersReading the manifest by eyeThis checker
Every container has a memory limit, not just a request.A block with a request already in it reads as resourced; the specific missing field is easy to not notice.Checks each of the four fields by name and reports exactly which is absent, per container.
No request exceeds its own limit for the same resource.Requires comparing two numbers that live in different blocks, sometimes several lines or containers apart.Parses both quantities and compares them directly, catching the exact case the API server rejects at apply time.
An init container's resources, not just the main containers'.Init containers are easy to skim past -- they run once and are not the "real" workload being reviewed.Checks init containers with the same four fields as regular containers.
A manifest with several workloads in one file.Attention naturally concentrates on the first or largest workload in a multi-document file.Analyzes every document independently and reports findings per workload.

Reviewing the manifest is not wrong -- it is how a team catches most problems, including ones this tool does not check at all (image tags, security context, probes). What it automates is the specific, mechanical comparison a visual pass is most likely to skip: is every field present, and does any request exceed its own limit.

Run the free resource-limits checker

The same worked example a visual review would pass

This is this tool's own bundled worked example -- the "Load worked example" button on the checker loads it verbatim:

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: checkout-api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: checkout-api
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: 512Mi
          limits:
            cpu: 500m
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: cache
  namespace: data
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: cache
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: 2
            memory: 4Gi
          limits:
            cpu: 1
            memory: 4Gi

Read start to finish, both containers look resourced: checkout-api has a memory request and a CPU limit set, and cache has requests and limits for both memory and CPU. Run this checker's own detection logic against it and it reports 2 workloads, 2 containers left unbounded or invalid, plus 3 more worth reviewing: checkout-api has no resources.limits.memory at all, despite having a memory request; and cache requests 2 CPUs while its own limit is 1 -- a value the API server rejects outright at kubectl apply, not a style note. Neither container's resources block is empty, so neither issue is the kind a quick "does this have limits set?" glance would catch.

Common questions

Isn't reading the manifest in review enough?

It catches anything visible on its own line -- a resources block missing entirely, an obviously wrong indent. It works less well for a container that has some requests or limits set (so the block looks present and reasonable) but is missing one specific field, or for two numbers that live a few lines apart in different blocks (a request under limits vs. a request under requests) that need to be compared against each other rather than read in isolation. Neither miss is a sign of a careless reviewer -- the YAML looks completely ordinary either way.

How easy is it really to miss a missing memory limit by eye?

In this tool's own bundled worked example, a Deployment's only container sets resources.requests.memory: 512Mi and resources.limits.cpu: 500m -- a resources block that is clearly not empty, with two real values in it. Nothing about reading it draws attention to the specific field that is absent: resources.limits.memory. A reviewer confirming 'yes, this has resource limits set' from a glance at the block is not wrong about what they saw; they are answering a coarser question than the one that matters.

Why is a request exceeding a limit easy to miss in review?

Because the two numbers being compared sit in different blocks -- requests.cpu and limits.cpu -- often several lines apart, sometimes in a different container's section entirely once a manifest has more than one workload. Each individual line reads as valid YAML with a valid quantity. The problem only exists in the relationship between the two values, and Kubernetes does not point it out until kubectl apply or helm upgrade fails admission validation -- after the review that would have caught it earlier has already passed.

Does this tool replace reviewing the manifest?

No, and it checks only resource requests and limits -- one narrow slice of everything a manifest review covers, such as image tags, security context, or probes. Reviewing the manifest is still how a team catches most problems and agrees the change makes sense. This tool exists for the specific, mechanical part of that review that benefits from being checked the same way every time: is every required field present, and does any request exceed its own limit.

See how this compares to a broader, deployed policy engine: this checker vs. Polaris. More on the mechanism behind each finding: why a missing resource limit takes down a node.

Evidence, not a determination. This tool reports what the manifest declares against a fixed set of documented Kubernetes mechanisms -- it cannot know what your workload actually needs at runtime, and a clean report is not a guarantee the values you set are the right ones. Verify against your own load-testing and Kubernetes' own resource-management documentation before relying on it.

Everything runs in your browser or as a local CLI. The manifest you load is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. why-a-missing-resource-limit-takes-down-.text:
← Back to Kubernetes Resource Limits Check

Why a missing resource limit can take down an entire node

Memory: two different mechanisms, depending on scope

A container with no memory limit is free to grow. Kubernetes itself does not stop it -- the only thing that eventually does is the Linux kernel's out-of-memory (OOM) killer, once the node runs genuinely short on memory. The OOM killer's scoring (oom_score_adj, weighted heavily by a cgroup's memory limit relative to what it is using) is not guaranteed to pick the container that grew; a process elsewhere on the node with a worse score can be the one killed instead.

Below that hard limit, Kubernetes' own kubelet runs node-pressure eviction: when a node crosses a memory (or disk) threshold, the kubelet evicts whole pods to relieve it, ranked first by QoS class (BestEffort evicted before Burstable, Burstable before Guaranteed) and then by how far each pod's actual usage exceeds its own requests. A container with no memory request at all is treated as requesting nothing, which makes any usage look maximally over-request -- ranking it for eviction first, regardless of how little it is actually using at that moment.

Ephemeral storage: the one most setups still miss

A container's logs, temporary files, and its own writable layer all draw on the node's local (ephemeral) storage, and Kubernetes tracks that the same way it tracks memory: as a resource a container can request and limit, documented under Resource Management for Pods and Containers. With no limit set, a container that logs too verbosely or leaves temp files behind can fill the node's disk. Once the node crosses its own disk-pressure threshold, the kubelet evicts pods to reclaim space -- again at the node level, not scoped to the container that filled it. Most teams reach for CPU and memory limits as a matter of habit and never add this one, because nothing prompts them to until a node has already gone into disk pressure.

CPU limits: a real trade-off, not a missing safety rail

CPU is different from memory and disk in one important way: it is compressible. A container over its CPU request is not killed, it is merely scheduled less. But a CPU limit, once set, is enforced by the kernel's CFS bandwidth controller, which grants a fixed quota once per scheduling period (by default 100 milliseconds) with no rollover of unused quota into the next period. A container with bursty usage -- busy for a slice of a period, idle for the rest, repeated -- can exhaust its quota partway through a period and be throttled for the remainder, even while the node as a whole has CPU sitting idle. This is tracked upstream as kubernetes/kubernetes#67577 and has led several engineering teams to publish their own "why we stopped setting CPU limits" write-ups after tracing latency spikes back to exactly this. It is not a reason to skip CPU limits everywhere -- strict multi-tenant isolation is a real, legitimate reason to keep them -- which is why this tool reports a set CPU limit as informational rather than as a problem: the point is to make the trade-off visible, not to make the decision for you.

The one this tool also catches: a request above its own limit

Kubernetes' API server validates, at admission time, that a container's resource request for a given type is never greater than its limit for that same type. A manifest that violates this is not deployed with a warning -- kubectl apply or a rolling helm upgrade is rejected outright. This is usually a typo (a limit lowered during a tuning pass without lowering the request to match, or the reverse) rather than a deliberate choice, and catching it before the apply step saves the round trip of a failed deploy.

What this tool looks for, and where it stops

It reads a manifest's YAML directly -- resources.requests and resources.limits on every container and init container across every Pod, Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, ReplicaSet, Job, and CronJob it finds -- and reports what is present, what is missing, and whether a request exceeds its own limit. It has no kubeconfig and makes no API server call, which is what makes it safe to run in CI against a manifest repository with no cluster credentials granted at all.

What it cannot do is tell you the right number for a request or limit -- that depends on what your workload actually uses, which only your own metrics (kubectl top, or whatever monitoring stack you run) can answer. It checks that a number is present and internally consistent, not that it is the correct one.

Common questions

What actually kills a container with no memory limit?

Two different mechanisms, depending on scope. If the container alone grows past what its node has free, the Linux kernel's out-of-memory killer picks a process to kill based on its own scoring -- not necessarily the container that grew, if another process on the node has a worse score. If the whole node is short on memory across many containers, the kubelet's own node-pressure eviction acts first, evicting whole pods ranked by QoS class and how far each is over its own requests -- a container with no request at all is ranked worst regardless of what it is actually using.

Why does an ephemeral-storage limit matter when memory and CPU are usually the ones people set?

Because a container's logs, temp files, and writable container layer all count against the node's local disk, and Kubernetes tracks that the same way it tracks memory: as a resource a container can request and limit. Skip the limit and a container that logs too verbosely, or writes temp files it never cleans up, can fill the node's disk. Once the node crosses its disk-pressure threshold the kubelet starts evicting pods to reclaim space -- not only the one that filled it, because eviction acts at the node level.

Should I always set a CPU limit along with the request?

Not automatically. A CPU limit is enforced through the kernel's CFS bandwidth controller, which grants a fixed quota once per scheduling period (typically 100ms) with no rollover of unused quota into the next period. A container with bursty CPU use -- busy for 20ms, idle for the rest of a period, repeated -- can be throttled inside that pattern even while the node as a whole has spare CPU sitting idle. This is a well-documented behaviour, tracked upstream as kubernetes/kubernetes#67577, and it is why several engineering teams have published posts about removing CPU limits while keeping CPU requests. A limit is still the right call for strict multi-tenant isolation; the point is that it is a trade-off to make deliberately, not a box to tick alongside every other resource field.
